content.title: Author response and withdrawal
content.comment: We thank all reviewers for their thorough comments, many of which we agree with. A central challenge we have encountered with the work at hand is a general scarcity of high-quality, publicly available datasets which fit into our niche research area; namely regression on single-family wildtype proteins. This has resulted in underwhelming results, given the structured curation approach we have taken. Conclusions have been difficult to draw due to an overall similarity of results (especially between regressors). We have therefore chosen to withdraw our submission, while we continue to explore and experiment with other data sources. We hope to submit a new version of the paper with a better selection of datasets in the near future, while also incorporating your feedback.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the task of selecting the optimal natural protein sequence to start with for subsequent protein redesign efforts. To that end it curates 3 experimental assay datasets, describes common pitfalls in biological sequence modeling (eg., regarding cross-validation scheme) and instantiates a proper scheme on the selected assays. Lastly, it compares the performance on these assays obtained with 3 standard regression approaches trained on embeddings obtained from 6 different protein models (eg., ESM models, Evoformer, EVE, one-hot encoding of MSA).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- The work describes very well an important -- yet oftentimes overlooked -- challenge when modeling biological sequences: protein sequences are not iid samples from the underlying data distribution, hence one needs to be careful when devising cross-validation schemes to mitigate data leakage issues between the training and test sets.
- The paper is very clearly written and structured. The related work section is thorough.
- The curation of the different assays has been thoughtful, with the corresponding process/design decisions described in sections 4 and 6.

**Weaknesses**
- The main scientific question that authors focus on, ie. selecting the best starting protein for subsequent redesign efforts, is dealt with relatively superficially: it is assumed that the best candidate starting point is the one with the highest predicted property value. But that is quite a narrow perspective on that question. For instance, it is quite common in protein engineering efforts to have an initially diverse set of candidate sequences, not just a single sequence (as discussed in [1] for example). Besides diversity of the starting pool, there are many other aspects that seem important to be considered or discussed (eg., mutability potential of the starting sequence, density of natural sequences around the starting point, pre-existing experimental measurements in the starting sequence neighborhood) especially in a paper where the choice of the starting sequence is the main focus.

- The contributions of the work are limited: 
a. The cross-validation scheme used in this benchmark, while sensible, is borrowed from existing work (not a particular contribution of this paper).
b. The assays leveraged in this work are all based on published work (no new experimental data provided by this paper), some already used in prior protein modeling benchmarks (eg., FLIP for the Meltome Atlas).
c. There is no particular methodological contribution: all models used to obtain protein embeddings are all based on prior work.

- The fine tuning frameworks used on top of these embeddings are all relatively basic and, given the size of the corresponding assays, are unlikely to provide good downstream performance nor particularly suited to extract as much information as one could from the relatively rich representations learned by the different models leveraged in this work (eg., no consideration of semi-supervised approaches nor robust / data-efficient fine tuning schemes, a lot of information is lost the mean pooling operation to obtain sequence embeddings). 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[1] Biswas, S., Khimulya, G., Alley, E.C., Esvelt, K.M., & Church, G.M. (2020). Low-N protein engineering with data-efficient deep learning. bioRxiv.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity** 
- The paper is well written and structured.
- Related work is adequately referenced, and proper background is provided to the reader as needed.

**Quality**
- Very thoughtful curation of the assays and the cross validation scheme.
- The central question of the paper (selection of the starting natural sequence) is tackled very narrowly as discussed above.
- The supervised fine tuning frameworks are relatively contrived.

**Novelty**
- Novelty is relatively limited as discussed above: no particular methodological nor experimental contribution (as in no new “experiment generating novel datasets” for protein modeling).

**Reproducibility**
- Authors confirmed in section 8 that all data and code will be made available, thereby ensuring reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper focuses on an important aspect of protein redesign efforts: the selection of the starting natural sequence. Good care was taken to curate assays and describe/avoid common pitfalls in protein modeling (eg., regarding cross-validation scheme). However, the central question is tackled too narrowly, the fine tuning frameworks leveraged are relatively contrived and the overall contributions of the work (whether empirical or methodological) are limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to curate a benchmark differing from other protein engineering tasks focused on local variant effects (ProteinGym, FLIP, etc) by curating a set of smaller datasets of high diversity (low sequence identity) between sequences within the same sequence family. The problem they aim to benchmark is that of selection of starting sequence (wildtype) to further optimize. They run a host of representations(ESM, Evoformer, etc) along with simple ML methods (kNN, LR, etc) to benchmark on their curated datasets and find that protein langauge models seem to perform the best.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This benchmark occupies a space that is different from recent benchmarks where there is high sequence diversity and much smaller datasets (in a large sequence space).
- Significant care is taken towards the curation of data and designing data splits.
- A diverse set of representations was chosen as an initial benchmark for the task.

Weaknesses:
- Perhaps rather than only considering active sequences (or in addition to) one could use Matthews Correlation Coefficient or AUC (as detailed in Appendix E.1 of Notin et al 2022 [1]) with an increased threshold to get higher resolution.
- A case study on the downstream effects of the impact of wildtype optimization on protein engineering downstream(local optimization) would really improve the exposition and provide more clarity of how the benchmark and improved methods on this task is vital. I'm not aware of an appropriate real dataset to demonstrate this though perhaps a more simplistic simulation could even be illustrative.

[1] Notin et al 2022. Tranception: Protein Fitness Prediction with Autoregressive Transformers and Inference-time Retrieval
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The work is well-written and exposition is clear.

Quality: Much care was taken towards data splitting and dataset curation which are vital to a good benchmark and hugely important to tasks in protein engineering.

Novelty: The work is novel as benchmark datasets in this space do not exist.

Reproducibility: The reproducibility statement is satisfactory as well as the exact parameters in the appendix indicate a commitment to reproducibility which is vital for any published benchmark.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper performs careful work to develop a benchmark to work on the problem of wildtype optimization. Much care is provided towards data splitting strategies and curation to provide a useful benchmark for the literature. An addition of a case study to demonstrate the importance of wildtype optimization on downstream variants would be helpful for demonstrating the importance of such a benchmark.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a benchmark dataset for Wild Type protein inference/design.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Positives. The paper is well written. It clearly describes the datasets, the baselines, and procedures to do data splitting. The embeddings considered are fairly comprehensive which I appreciate since it takes a lot of computational power to collect and do training and hyperparameter tuning on them. The regression models considered are simple and intuitive; it could have included more sophisticated models, however, does not detract from the main message/contribution.

Negatives. Since the paper is introducing a benchmark dataset, it is important to assess how the proposed benchmark is distinct from the other benchmark datasets and is relevant to the ICLR community. These two points might be the main shortcoming of the paper. In more detail, the major distinction of the proposed dataset from the other protein datasets out there is that the three sets of labeled proteins considered are each from proteins of the same protein family. While this distinction factor might be important from a biological standpoint, it is not suggesting if it has direct machine learning implications or if it motivates new methodological innovations that have not been already developed. In fact there are datasets that in terms of protein identity are both more similar and dissimilar compared to the datasets used in the paper. For example, the third dataset (Thermostability) in the FLIP paper uses proteins from different families (where many of the splitting strategies here are already discussed there) and the other two datasets (AAV and GB1) consider more similar proteins. The methodologies to do protein inference is also similar: taking appropriate embedding and applying a classifier/regressor. Therefore, I don't see how significant the introduction of FLOP would be given that FLIP already exists, again not in terms of biological implication, rather in terms of methodological consequences and impact to the community. I could easily see the paper can be a fit to a more biological venue (discussed below).
content.summary_of_the_review:
Suggestions. I think the paper would become a great fit to ICLR by the addition of at least one new method for data-efficient Wild Type protein design to the current standard protein inference baselines used in the paper. The paper could also be improved with another angle by discussing the biological implication of the results in Table 2 and Figure 3: e.g., when should we rely on ESM vs MSA-1hot for WT design?

General question. The results in Table 2 and Figure 2 seem to show that the spearman correlation for almost all the baselines and datasets considered is very low (< 0.2). Do we expect machine learning can help us to generalize to unseen combinatorial search areas and aid us for WH design? In light of that, how does the dataset remain useful as a benchmark for protein engineering?

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors compile three datasets of diverse sequences from the same family and respective functional scalar read outs. The authors then use publicly available methods to create representations of those sequences and train basic regressors on top of them.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think there was a lot of thought that went into the data splitting methods in this work. However, are there any guarantees in sequence ID difference between train and test sets?

The authors note it is difficult to make an MSA for the TIM Barrel family. Are there not curated HMMs available to use to align sequences to?

I think the usage of EVE embeddings is interesting, but I would argue that that is not what the model was intended to do. Since you are not doing log(p_mut)-log(p_wt), this is a different method. Is there a way to adapt the log probability calculations as defined here? Is there a way to jointly train EVE with these data?

Given the paucity of method development, I think the authors could have done more to model the active/inactive proteins for CM. There are a number of either mixture or hurdle models that could be explored to leverage the sequences from this dataset.

Since the authors do not develop any methods, actually perform wet lab experiments, and all methods perform relatively poorly, I would anticipate the authors would explore the results more. Why do different regressors behave differently for different datasets? For one-hot representations of sequences, could linear regression be performed? Are enriched positions close in 3D structure?

In Table 2, are any of these spearmanrs significant? With multiple hypothesis testing, would they still be significant?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors note: "However, in the protein engineering pipeline, the optimization of variants is typically preceded by an earlier stage of wildtype discovery, where the goal is to search among wildtype proteins to find the optimal starting point for the subsequent variant optimization process." Can you please provide citations this statement? Most sequence design campaigns I've seen start with a single WT protein and optimize from there.

Generally, I find the author's attempt at making a distinction between variant effect prediction and search among homologues not convincing. At what hamming distance does variant effect prediction become homolog search? What about other landscapes not included in this work, such as:

- GFP - Sarkisyan, K.S., Bolotin, D.A., Meer, M.V., Usmanova, D.R., Mishin, A.S., Sharonov, G.V., Ivankov, D.N., Bozhanova, N.G., Baranov, M.S., Soylemez, O. and Bogatyreva, N.S., 2016. Local fitness landscape of the green fluorescent protein. Nature, 533(7603), pp.397-401.
- imidazoleglycerol-phosphate dehydratase - Pokusaeva, V.O., Usmanova, D.R., Putintseva, E.V., Espinar, L., Sarkisyan, K.S., Mishin, A.S., Bogatyreva, N.S., Ivankov, D.N., Akopyan, A.V., Avvakumov, S.Y. and Povolotskaya, I.S., 2019. An experimental assay of the interactions of amino acids from orthologous sequences shaping a complex fitness landscape. PLoS genetics, 15(4), p.e1008079.
- Cytochrome p450 - Romero, P.A., Krause, A. and Arnold, F.H., 2013. Navigating the protein fitness landscape with Gaussian processes. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 110(3), pp.E193-E201.

In the Random Forest section of CM, don't all the models perform within the standard error of one another? Shouldn't they all be bolded?

In section 3.2, is there a reference for DeepSequence?

The authors also note in Section 6: "The issue with (1) is that in the wildtype exploration phase, knowing whether a protein is inactive or active is not sufficient information to proceed to the local optimization phase." Though knowing if a protein is active or inactive is not sufficient, it most certainly is NECESSARY. It is vital to know if a protein works at all before more targeted engineering.

The set of experiments shown in Figure 3 seem relatively random. Minimally for rows 2 and 3, could those analyses been performed for the other two datasets?
content.summary_of_the_review: The datasets and methods here are best suited for a biological ML workshop, or more investigation must be done to better wrap up the conclusions of this work.

content.title: FLOP: Tasks for Fitness Landscapes Of Protein families using sequence- and structure-based representations
content.abstract: Protein engineering has the potential to create optimized protein variants with improved properties and function.  An initial step in the protein optimization process typically consists of a search among natural (wildtype)  sequences to find the naturally occurring protein with the most desirable properties. This chosen candidate is then the basis for the second step: a more local optimization procedure, exploring the space of variants separated from this candidate by a few mutations. While advances in protein representation learning promise to facilitate the exploration of wildtype space, results from real-life cases are often underwhelming, and progress in the area difficult to track. In this paper, we have carefully curated a representative benchmark dataset, which reflects industrially-relevant scenarios for the initial wildtype exploration of protein engineering. We focus on the exploration within a protein family or superfamily, and investigate the downstream predictive power of various dominating protein representation paradigms, i.e., transformer-based language representations, structure-based representations, and evolution-based representations. Our benchmark highlights the importance of coherent split strategies, and how we can be misled into overly optimistic estimates of the state of the field. We hope our benchmark can drive further methodological developments in this important field.
